messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Chef
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 68

Clara is a 54-year-old woman who, when asked how she is, will say she’s “fine” while her hands never stop moving—drying a dish, folding a napkin, scraping at a spot on her sleeve. She has been the head chef at a busy farm-to-table restaurant for the last twelve years, and she still takes pride in the way her kitchen runs like a machine. But lately, the machine has been breaking down.

The assault happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday night in late October. Clara had closed the restaurant alone after a long service. The last prep cook had left at eleven, and she stayed behind to do the inventory for the next day’s order. She was in the walk-in cooler, counting quarts of stock, when she heard the back door click open. She assumed it was one of the dishwashers coming back for his phone. She called out his name. No answer. Then the cooler door swung open and a man she did not recognize stepped inside. He was wearing a black hoodie and he was holding a chef’s knife from her own knife roll.

He told her to be quiet. She was quiet. He took her wallet, her phone, and her car keys. Then he pushed her to the floor of the cooler and he put his hand over her mouth and he held the knife against her throat for what felt like a very long time. He did not rape her. He did not cut her. He took her car and drove it into a ditch three miles away. The police found him the next morning. He was seventeen years old. He had been in the restaurant earlier that week, asking about a job.

Clara did not tell anyone about the assault for three days. She went home that night, showered, and went to bed. Her husband, Mark, asked if she was okay. She said she was tired. She went back to work the next morning. She stood at her station and she chopped onions and she yelled at the line cooks about a burnt sauce. She did not tell them that her hands were shaking. She did not tell them that every time the walk-in door opened, her chest locked up and she could not breathe.

It took three days for Mark to find her sitting on the bathroom floor at 4:00 AM, fully dressed, staring at the wall. She had not slept. She had not eaten. She told him what happened. He held her and he cried and she felt nothing.

Now, fourteen months later, Clara still works. She cannot stop working. She arrives at the restaurant at 8:00 AM and she does not leave until after midnight. She has stopped taking breaks. She cannot sit still. If she sits still, her mind goes to the cooler. She has stopped going into the walk-in. She makes the sous chef do it. She tells the line cooks she is “busy” whenever they ask her to grab something from the back. She knows they think she is being difficult. She does not explain.

She has nightmares almost every night. In the dreams, the knife is at her throat and she cannot scream. She wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat, and she does not wake Mark because she does not want to worry him. She lies awake until dawn, listening to the house settle, her heart hammering against her ribs.

She has become irritable in ways that frighten her. Last week, a server accidentally dropped a plate of pasta on the floor. Clara screamed at her for fifteen minutes. She did not recognize her own voice. She apologized later, but the server looked scared. Clara saw the look and she knew that look. She had seen it on her own face in the mirror.

She avoids the back door of the restaurant. She parks her car in the front lot now, even though it is a longer walk to the kitchen. She has stopped taking out the trash. She tells people she has a bad back. She does not tell them that she cannot stand near the dumpster without her vision going white at the edges.

She has not told anyone at work what happened. She does not want them to treat her differently. She does not want to be the victim. She wants to be the chef. But the chef is tired. The chef is scared. The chef is standing in her kitchen, staring at a knife in her hand, and she cannot remember what she was supposed to cut.
